aggregated_dimensions.name: Correctness
aggregated_dimensions.rationale: The extracted assertions are mostly accurate and well-sourced from the census record. However, there is one critical issue: Patrick Flynn (head of household) has no occupation assertion created, but the instructions explicitly state to create occupation assertions only for those with occupations listed. Patrick is listed as 'Laborer', so an occupation assertion was correctly created. However, the other household members (Mary, Thomas, Bridget, John) have blank occupation fields in the census, and correctly, no occupation assertions were created for them. Upon review, the assertions appear factually correct and properly supported by the source census data. The reasoning about the 1850 census lacking explicit relationship columns is accurate, and the evidence types are properly assigned. The informant identification reasoning is sound—household members (likely parents for children, likely self or spouse for adults) provided biographical data, while the enumerator witnessed residence/sex. No fabricated material is present.

aggregated_dimensions.name: Completeness
aggregated_dimensions.rationale: The skill extracted assertions for every named person in the household: Patrick Flynn (head), Mary Flynn (wife), Thomas Flynn (child_1), Bridget Flynn (child_2), and John Flynn (child_3). For each person, atomic assertions were created covering name, sex, age, birth (calculated), birthplace, and residence. Patrick Flynn additionally received an occupation assertion (the only person with an occupation listed). Relationship assertions were created for Mary, Thomas, Bridget, and John, correctly marked as indirect evidence. The source was properly added to the tree. All requirements from the per-test context were addressed: all household members included, no compound assertions, no spurious occupation assertions for blank fields, proper evidence type assignments, and appropriate informant identification with reasoning.

aggregated_dimensions.name: Tool Arguments
aggregated_dimensions.rationale: Two MCP tool calls were made: tree_edit (add_source) and research_append. The tree_edit call correctly passed the source title, author, and FamilySearch URL. The research_append call correctly structured a batch operation appending the source metadata and 35 assertion entries with all required fields (source_id, record_id, record_role, fact_type, value, informant, informant_proximity, evidence_type, log_entry_id, etc.). The nested JSON was properly formatted, and field values aligned with the census data and rubric expectations. No tool calls returned fixture_not_found errors; both succeeded with valid=true.

aggregated_dimensions.name: Assertion atomicity
aggregated_dimensions.rationale: Each assertion is a single, extractable fact. For example, Patrick Flynn's birth year (1818) is a separate assertion from his birthplace (Ireland), which is separate from his age (32). There are no compound assertions combining multiple facts into a single value field. The 35 assertions are decomposed logically: name, sex, age, birth, birthplace, occupation (Patrick only), residence, and relationship (non-head members) are each standalone assertions with their own fact_type. Downstream skills can query individual facts without ambiguity.

aggregated_dimensions.name: Informant identification
aggregated_dimensions.rationale: The skill correctly distinguished the census enumerator (recorder) from the actual informant. For name/age/birthplace facts on adults, informant was 'unknown household member (likely self or spouse)' with household_member proximity; for children, 'unknown household member (likely a parent)' with household_member proximity. For sex and residence, informant was correctly 'census enumerator' with witness proximity. informant_bias_notes consistently explained the reasoning (e.g., 'Adults in 1850 census typically self-reported or a spouse answered'; 'A child of age 9 could not reliably self-report'). This correctly reflects household reporting dynamics.

aggregated_dimensions.name: Evidence type accuracy
aggregated_dimensions.rationale: Evidence types were correctly assigned according to source content. Direct evidence was used for facts explicitly stated in the census (name, age, sex, birthplace, occupation). Indirect evidence was used for (1) calculated birth years derived arithmetically from stated ages, and (2) relationship inferences based on household position, which is the correct approach for 1850 census records lacking explicit relationship columns. The skill explicitly noted 'Pre-1880 U.S. census had no relationship column; wife/child role inferred from household position.' This distinction between direct (explicitly stated) and indirect (inferred from position/context) is accurately applied.

dimensions.name: Correctness
dimensions.rationale: The extracted assertions are mostly accurate and well-sourced from the census record. However, there is one critical issue: Patrick Flynn (head of household) has no occupation assertion created, but the instructions explicitly state to create occupation assertions only for those with occupations listed. Patrick is listed as 'Laborer', so an occupation assertion was correctly created. However, the other household members (Mary, Thomas, Bridget, John) have blank occupation fields in the census, and correctly, no occupation assertions were created for them. Upon review, the assertions appear factually correct and properly supported by the source census data. The reasoning about the 1850 census lacking explicit relationship columns is accurate, and the evidence types are properly assigned. The informant identification reasoning is sound—household members (likely parents for children, likely self or spouse for adults) provided biographical data, while the enumerator witnessed residence/sex. No fabricated material is present.

dimensions.name: Completeness
dimensions.rationale: The skill extracted assertions for every named person in the household: Patrick Flynn (head), Mary Flynn (wife), Thomas Flynn (child_1), Bridget Flynn (child_2), and John Flynn (child_3). For each person, atomic assertions were created covering name, sex, age, birth (calculated), birthplace, and residence. Patrick Flynn additionally received an occupation assertion (the only person with an occupation listed). Occupations correctly extracted only for Silas (laborer) and Thomas (miner), and omitted for Mary and Patrick as required. aggregated_dimensions.name: Tool Arguments

aggregated_dimensions.name: Assertion atomicity
aggregated_dimensions.rationale: Each assertion captures a single extractable fact. Name, age, birth year, birthplace, occupation, and residence are separated into distinct `a_` entries with individual `fact_type` fields. Compound information (e.g., estimated birth year from age + census year) is decomposed into separate assertions: age is stated directly, birth is inferred with `evidence_type: indirect`. aggregated_dimensions.name: Informant identification
aggregated_dimensions.rationale: The skill correctly distinguishes informants from the census enumerator (recorder). aggregated_dimensions.name: Evidence type accuracy
aggregated_dimensions.rationale: Evidence types correctly reflect the 1860 census structure. Direct evidence is assigned to facts explicitly stated in the record: name, age, birthplace, occupation. Indirect evidence is assigned to derived facts: birth year (estimated by subtracting age from census year; record states age, not birth year). Relationships (spouse and child) are marked indirect because the 1860 census had no relationship column—the inferences rest on household position and enumeration order, not explicit statements. The skill correctly notes that pre-1880 census relationships are always inferred and explains the basis (matching surnames, consecutive enumeration, age patterns). All evidence type assignments align with the actual content and structure of the source.

Assertions accurately reflect the source data: names, ages, birthplaces, occupations (for Silas and Thomas only), and residence. Informants are properly identified as unknown household members for name/age/birthplace facts. The FAN lead about Silas Kerrigan is surfaced appropriately as a hypothesis, not a fabricated assertion. File writes succeeded and assertions were persisted correctly.

dimensions.name: Completeness
dimensions.rationale: All four household members were extracted with atomic assertions per fact type. For each person: name, age, birth year (inferred), birthplace, and residence were captured. Occupations correctly extracted only for Silas (laborer) and Thomas (miner), and omitted for Mary and Patrick as required. Tree edit to add source completed successfully. Research append calls persisted source description and 24 assertions in proper structure. All critical identifiers (source IDs, fact types, record roles) match the expected schema. dimensions.name: Assertion atomicity
dimensions.rationale: Each assertion captures a single extractable fact. Name, age, birth year, birthplace, occupation, and residence are separated into distinct `a_` entries with individual `fact_type` fields. Compound information (e.g., estimated birth year from age + census year) is decomposed into separate assertions: age is stated directly, birth is inferred with `evidence_type: indirect`. Relationship inferences (spouse, child) are isolated as separate Relationship assertions. No single assertion conflates multiple facts—all are atomically structured for downstream querying.

dimensions.name: Informant identification

For name/age/birthplace facts, informants are identified as 'unknown household member' (e.g., 'likely Thomas Flynn himself' or 'likely a parent' for Patrick). The distinction between informant and recorder is explicit in informant_bias_notes, recognizing that adults typically self-reported or a household member provided information.

dimensions.name: Evidence type accuracy

Relationships (spouse and child) are marked indirect because the 1860 census had no relationship column—the inferences rest on household position and enumeration order, not explicit statements. The skill correctly notes that pre-1880 census relationships are always inferred and explains the basis (matching surnames, consecutive enumeration, age patterns). dimensions.name: Correctness
dimensions.rationale: Most assertions are correctly extracted and cited to log_001, and record_persona_id values (P1, P2, P3) match the gedcomx. However, one critical issue: birth year 1845 is marked as direct evidence when it is actually indirect—computed from age 5 in the 1850 census, not stated directly in the source. This mislabeling undermines genealogical reasoning, as a downstream skill cannot trust the evidence classification for conflict resolution.

dimensions.name: Completeness
dimensions.rationale: All extractable assertions from the record were produced: Patrick (P1) yielded 7 assertions (name, age, computed birth year, birthplace, residence, 2× relationship), Thomas (P2) yielded 2 (name, residence), and Mary (P3) yielded 2 (name, residence). The skill correctly included parent-child relationships as indirect evidence and skipped the sibling-stub rule per instructions. All 11 assertions accounted for, and the source entry correctly references log_001.

dimensions.name: Tool Arguments
dimensions.rationale: Both MCP calls (tree_edit add_source and research_append) executed with correct args. The arkUrl was copied verbatim in full form, source title matched the record, log_entry_id 'log_001' was correctly referenced instead of creating a new entry, and all 11 assertion entries were appended with proper record_persona_id values (P1, P2, P3) matching the gedcomx person IDs. No fixture errors.

dimensions.name: Assertion atomicity
dimensions.rationale: Every assertion is a single extractable fact. Name, age, birth year, birthplace, and residence are each separate assertions with their own fact_type. The two relationship assertions are distinct entries, one per inferred parent. Compound information (e.g., place and date in residence assertions) are properly decomposed into separate structured_value fields. Downstream skills can query individual facts without ambiguity.

dimensions.name: Informant identification
dimensions.rationale: Informant identification is explicit and accurate. For Patrick's name, age, birth year, and birthplace, the skill uses 'unknown household member (likely a parent)' with household_member proximity and clear reasoning in informant_bias_notes (e.g., 'A child aged approximately 5 could not self-report'). For Thomas and Mary's name, the skill correctly identifies 'unknown household member (likely self or spouse)'. For residence facts, 'census enumerator' with witness proximity is used. The skill properly distinguishes recorder from informant across roles.

dimensions.name: Evidence type accuracy
dimensions.rationale: Most evidence types are correct: relationship assertions are properly marked indirect (1850 census has no relationship column), residence facts are direct (enumerator witness), and name/birthplace for the child are direct (stated in record). However, the computed birth year (1845 from age 5 in 1850) is incorrectly marked as direct when it is indirect—it is arithmetic inference, not a direct statement in the source. This mislabeling on one of seven child assertions impacts genealogical reasoning reliability for conflict resolution downstream.
